summary:
Ohio is a state within the United States, so a visitor stands first under the national framework: Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to correct the application of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Entry screening carries an outing risk that applies at every United States port of entry, including Ohio's airports. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the country to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating an applicant who lists a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Ohio's principal own measure concerns facilities. Governor Mike DeWine signed Senate Bill 104, the Protect All Students Act, on 27 November 2024; it took effect on 25 February 2025, ninety days after signing. The statute requires every public and private K-12 school, college and university in Ohio to designate restrooms, locker rooms, changing and shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of males or females on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, which in practice directs trans students to facilities matching their birth-certificate sex.

The Ohio statute contains no enforcement mechanism. It was signed out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil-rights groups, and was sponsored by Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino.

A national legal risk assessment published 27 August 2026 places Ohio in its worst-graded group of fifteen states, a tier below the four states flagged Do Not Travel (Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas), under a national frame of worst policies in effect.

Wider national exposure remains relevant to a visitor who is detained or needs care. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, some hospitals paused care, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
tangentialFactors:
Ohio's placement in a fifteen-state worst tier is a comparison point rather than an outlier: the same July 2026 assessment groups Ohio with Alabama, Arkansas, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, North Dakota, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming, and ranks all of them below Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas, which are flagged Do Not Travel.

Ohio's statute belongs to a wider national pattern of facility restriction. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban; some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Idaho's felony bathroom ban carries up to five years and is partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists, and Kansas operates a bounty-hunter civil-suit regime; rights groups describe Kansas's February 2026 document law as a template other states may copy.

Enforcement elsewhere has escalated quickly enough to shape expectations in Ohio. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states nationally, and a July 2026 assessment reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.
localsOnly:
Ohio's facility obligations bind institutions rather than individuals: every public and private K-12 school, college and university in the state must designate restrooms, locker rooms, changing rooms, shower rooms and overnight accommodations for exclusive male or female use on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth.

Senate Bill 104, formally the Protect All Students Act and widely called the state's bathroom bill, was sponsored by Republican state Senator Jerry Cirino, signed by Governor Mike DeWine on 27 November 2024 and took effect on 25 February 2025.

The statute contains no enforcement mechanism, so its operation depends on institutional designation rather than a stated penalty or complaint procedure. The Governor signed it out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil-rights groups.
